title: Review of Tenses & Simple Sentences
subtitle: Choosing a tense, and making a sentence stand up.
objectives: Choose the right tense for a sentence
Keep one tense across a piece of writing
Spot a fragment and fix it

cards.title: Three tenses, and sentences that actually finish
cards.text: You have past, present and future. The other half of writing is making each sentence stand up on its own.

cards.title: The time word usually decides for you
cards.text: Find the marker, then match the verb.
points: **Yesterday, last week** → simple past.
**Every day, usually** → simple present.
**Tomorrow, next month** → a future form.
**No marker?** Then the surrounding sentences decide.

question.text: 'Every morning he ____ for an hour.' Which fits?
question.explain: 'Every morning' is a habit, so simple present: runs.

cards.title: It needs a subject and a verb, and it must finish a thought
points: **Subject** — who or what the sentence is about.
**Verb** — what they did, do or will do.
**The blades spun.** Two words, complete.
**Because the bearing was dry.** Not complete. It leaves you waiting.

question.text: 'After I unplugged the fan.' is a complete sentence.
question.explain: It has a subject and a verb but it does not finish the thought. 'After' leaves you hanging.

cards.title: Write up a repair in three tenses
cards.text: The same job, told three ways, and each one is correct for its moment.
points: **Past:** I replaced the capacitor and it started.
**Present:** It runs on all three speeds now.
**Future:** I am going to oil the bearings next.
**One tense per sentence.** Switch between sentences, not inside them.

cards.title: The commonest fault, and an easy fix
cards.text: A fragment is a piece of a sentence pretending to be whole.
points: **Usually starts with** because, although, when, after, since.
**Fix it** by attaching it to a full sentence.
**'Because it overheated.'** → *It cut out because it overheated.*
**Read it alone.** If you are still waiting, it is a fragment.

cards.title: One verb, three places
cards.text: Watch the bar move across NOW. Sliding between them mid-sentence is the fault.

cards.title: A race report uses all three and never mixes them
cards.text: Past for what happened, present for the standings, future for the next round.
points: **He took pole on Saturday.** Past.
**He leads the championship by four points.** Present.
**He will start from the front next week.** Future.
**Three sentences, three tenses, no confusion.**

question.explain: Subject and verb, and the thought finishes. The other three leave you waiting.

cards.title: Literature Review: Don Quixote, Chapter 15: Sancho Panza on the Road
cards.text: Sancho travels alone and spends most of the chapter arguing with himself about what to tell his master.
points: **He had not delivered the letter.** Past.
**He is deciding what to invent.** Present.
**He will report that Dulcinea was winnowing wheat.** Future.
**Cervantes moves between tenses** sentence by sentence, never inside one.

cards.title: Past, present, future
cards.alt: Three candles in a row: new and unlit, burning and half melted, and burnt down to a cold stub
cards.text: Burnt out, burning, not yet lit. Three tenses with no grammar in sight.

terms.def: One subject, one verb, one complete thought.
A piece of a sentence that does not finish its thought.
Who or what the sentence is about.
Not changing tense partway through a sentence.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Find the time marker and the tense follows.
A sentence needs a subject, a verb and a finished thought.
Fragments usually begin with because, although, when or after.
Change tense between sentences, never inside one.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 5 English, the scope's review week, which pairs tense choice with sentence completeness because the two faults appear together in his writing. Tense selection is taught as marker-matching, which is reliable and fast. The fragment section is the more valuable half: fragments are named by their usual opening words — because, although, when, after — and the read-it-alone test is given as the check. The repair write-up card shows all three tenses used correctly in sequence, which models the rule that tense changes between sentences, not inside them.
discussion: What is the quickest way to pick a tense?
Why is 'Because it overheated.' not a sentence?
When is it fine to change tense?
extension: Write a repair or a match report in three sentences, one per tense.
Find three fragments in your own writing and fix them.
misconceptions: Thinking a long phrase must be a sentence.
Treating a dependent clause as complete.
